en.title: When deterrence fails: NATO, Russia and the political economy of a major-power war
en.deck: A comprehensive examination of how a direct great-power confrontation could transform military deterrence, nuclear risk, technology, finance, production, energy, media, societies, collective psychology and negotiated peace, with a critical reading of the actual 2026 threat assessments.
keywords: global war risk assessment Danish intelligence Estonia
major power war economic psychosocial effects
long war armistice peace settlement duration
en.regime: Rising risk of limited military incidents within enduring nuclear deterrence; substantial industrial mobilisation without evidence that broad war is predetermined.
en.key_risk: A limited incident, ambiguous attribution or disruption could trigger uncontrolled escalation, while prolonged conflict corrodes civilian infrastructure, trust, budgets and human capital.
watch: Verified limited-incursion evidence and Article 4 consultation outcomes
Independent attribution of air, maritime, cyber and infrastructure incidents
Actual defence deliveries and readiness relative to procurement targets
Nuclear risk reduction arrangements after New START expiration
Civilian casualties, displacement, school/medical continuity and energy shipping
Verified crisis communications, arms-control negotiations and monitored settlements

pt-BR.deck: Pesquisa aprofundada sobre como um confronto entre potências afetaria dissuasão nuclear, armamentos, tecnologia, finanças, produção, energia, mídia, sociedades, psicologia coletiva e acordos de paz, confrontando cenários com avaliações oficiais de 2026.

contrary_evidence: February 2026 Estonian foreign intelligence assessed no Russian intention to attack NATO within the following year.
September 2026 Danish intelligence described a broad conventional invasion as highly unlikely and no visible preparation, while noting low but rising risk of limited military attack.
NATO's defence commitments and nuclear deterrence can reduce incentives for deliberate major war even while proximity and incidents create risk.
limitations: A hypothetical war has no empirically justifiable start date, duration, nuclear escalation probability or global casualty count.
Intelligence judgments reflect limited horizons, assumptions and possible unknown decision-making; they are not direct measurements of all state intentions.
SIPRI military spending, nuclear inventories and capacity figures are estimates; monetary totals do not measure theatre-specific operational readiness.
Scenario horizons are conceptual and not likelihood weights; economic and psychological consequences require country- and group-specific exposure data.
Historical background and contemporary incident attribution are distinct evidentiary tasks; no claimed anonymous sabotage is treated as verified.
